nameStory: The 'upswept moonwort' gets its name from the distinctive way its fertile frond segments angle upward, as if swept skyward by an invisible hand. The 'moonwort' part comes from the crescent or moon-shaped segments found on many species in this ancient fern family, though this particular species has more triangular leaflets.
description: Upswept moonwort is a tiny, mysterious fern that's easy to overlook in the wild. This diminutive plant sends up a single yellowish-green frond that rarely exceeds 6 centimeters (about 2.5 inches) tall from its underground stem. Unlike typical ferns, it has a unique two-part structure: one section looks like a miniature fan-shaped leaf, while the other bears tiny grape-like clusters that release spores. It's so small and uncommon that spotting one feels like discovering a hidden treasure.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Single yellowish-green frond divided into two distinct parts - one sterile leafy section with fan or wedge-shaped segments, and one fertile section with tiny grape-like spore clusters

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Extremely small plant, typically under 2.5 inches tall, growing as a solitary frond from underground rather than in clumps like most ferns

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores housed in tiny round clusters that look like miniature grapes on the fertile portion, quite different from the dots or lines of typical ferns

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in open, grassy areas near water rather than shady forest floors where most ferns grow

habitat: Look for upswept moonwort in grassy areas near rivers, streams, or wetlands rather than deep forest shade. It prefers open, moist ground where grasses and wildflowers grow, often in areas that flood seasonally. With only 9 recorded observations in all of New England, this is one of our region's rarest ferns.

seasonality.spring: The single frond emerges directly from the ground without the typical fiddlehead coiling of other ferns. Look for the distinctive yellowish-green color in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing time when the fan-shaped sterile leaflets are fully developed and the grape-like spore clusters are most visible on the fertile portion.
seasonality.fall: Fronds begin to yellow and wither as spores are released. The entire above-ground portion dies back completely.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground growth visible; the plant retreats entirely underground to its persistent root system until next year's emergence.

funFact: Upswept moonwort belongs to one of the most ancient fern families on Earth, with relatives that grew alongside the dinosaurs over 100 million years ago - yet this tiny plant wasn't scientifically described until relatively recently because it's so easily overlooked!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be mistaken for a small flowering plant or grass seedling rather than other ferns due to its tiny size and unusual two-part structure. The grape-like spore clusters are the giveaway - no flowering plant has anything quite like them.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'moonworts' and 'grapeferns,' these plants are true ferns that reproduce by spores, not seeds like grapes. The common names reflect their unique appearance rather than any relationship to lunar cycles or grape vines.
compareHints: Upswept moonwort differs from other moonworts by its fan or wedge-shaped leaflet segments that angle upward, rather than the more rounded or deeply divided segments of relatives like matricary grapefern. It's also among the smallest in the genus, and its preference for grassy riverside areas sets it apart from woodland species like little grapefern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Matricary grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its chamomile-like leaf segments that are more finely divided than most of its relatives.
Narrow triangle moonwort differs from matricary grapefern by having much narrower, more pointed segments rather than finely dissected, lacy ones.
**[Uncertain claim flagged: specific comparison details]** Swamp moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for wet habitats and its small, fan-shaped sterile frond segments.
Little grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its simple, often undivided leaf blade, whereas matricary grapefern and others have multiple leaflets or more complex divisions.
Unlike its moonwort relatives with their more typical triangular or oval leaflet shapes, spathulate moonwort's spatula-shaped segments are unmistakable.
Prairie moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for dry, prairie-like conditions rather than the moist, shaded habitats preferred by most of its relatives.
